snippets.text: Fixed obstructions that occlude less than 70% of a coronary vessel lumen typically are asymptomatic, even with exertion. In comparison, lesions that occlude more than 70% of a vessel lumen—resulting in so-called “critical stenosis”—generally cause symptoms in the setting of increased demand; with critical stenosis, certain levels of exertion predictably cause chest pain, and the patient is said to have stable angina. A fixed stenosis that occludes 90% or more of a vascular lumen can lead to inadequate coronary blood flow with symptoms even at rest—one of the forms ofunstable angina (see “ ” later in the chapter).

snippets.text: In general, historical findings depend on the stage of coronary artery occlusion. The symptoms are related to myocardial ischemia or myocardial contractility.[17] Patients can present with chest pain, shortness of breath, or tiredness. Patients with subtotal occlusion complain of chest pain, shortness of breath aggravated by exertion, and easy fatiguability. The symptoms usually resolve at rest. However, patients with total occlusion of the coronary arteries have symptoms at rest and are refractory to medical therapy. Clinicians should take a detailed history to rule in or rule out important risk factors, ie, family history, smoking, obesity, high blood pressure, decreased physical activity, excessive alcohol, diabetes, and a sedentary lifestyle. Physical examination includes a complete general physical examination to look for xanthomas and a general assessment of blood circulation, followed by a detailed cardiovascular examination.

snippets.text: The workup of modifiable ACLR graft failure remains challenging, even before surgical planning for revision ACLR.
